Quantitative research note · FTSE daily bars

Trend-Line Swing Trading, Tested

A popular support/resistance breakout method, implemented faithfully and measured against a proper cost model. The idea is clean and fully mechanisable — and it does not work.

Lance Walton · 6 September 2026 · 20 FTSE names · ~26 years · spread-bet costs

Verdict

The method, as it can be faithfully specified on daily bars, has negative expectancy before costs, and the result is robust to every lever it exposes — the volatility band, the trend-line length filter, and the exit rule. It is a rigorously falsified idea.

01 — THE IDEA

Straight lines under lows, over highs

Draw support lines through swing lows and resistance lines through swing highs, extend them forward as rays, and trade the breakouts: go long when price breaks the nearest resistance, exit when it breaks the opposing support (the "safety line"), trailing that line to lock in profit. It is the archetypal chart-trader's method — and, unusually, precise enough to test without discretion.

The claim under test is a specific author's: that this, traded on a short timeframe, makes money. We test the structure and rules exactly as described, on daily bars, and let the numbers speak.

02 — STRUCTURE

The lines are a convex hull

The construction has a clean identity: the support lines are exactly the lower convex hull of the lows (anchored on the all-time low, gradients increasing); resistance is the upper hull of the highs. That makes the whole structure layer deterministic, parameter-free, and O(n) to compute — every tunable choice lives later, in the signal layer. We work in ln(price), so a straight line is constant % growth.

One data note that matters more than it should: the method anchors on the single global extreme, so a single bad tick rewrites everything. BP printed a low of 4.7p on 2019-12-13 while trading around £4.61 — one glitch that hijacked 26 years of support structure until it was repaired.

03 — SIGNALS

Frequent, and firing both ways

Closeness — for a "touch" of a line, and for a "breach" of it — is set by one pre-registered band, k · ATR (14-day Wilder ATR), evaluated in price space. An entry needs the action line to have at least three touches, then a breakout beyond the band. Walked forward with no look-ahead, the signals come thick and in both directions through sideways tape — an early sign the breakouts are being read from noise.

04 — THE BACKTEST

Every name loses; buy & hold wins

The full simulator enters at the next open, trails the safety-line stop with an ATR disaster-floor, takes one position at a time, and prices a spread-bet wrapper: 10 bps/side spread plus 5%/yr financing, no UK stamp duty. Twenty liquid, sector-varied FTSE names, ~26 years each.

Base case, k = 0.5value
Names profitable0 / 20
Median strategy total−83%
Median buy & hold+251%
Pooled win rate14.4%
Mean net return / trade−0.30%
Profit factor0.39
 Across ~11,900 trades. Profit factor below 1.0 means gross losses exceed gross wins.

The k-sweep — our pre-registered robustness check — never crosses into profit: profit factor sits at 0.38–0.45 for every k ∈ {0.25 … 1.5}, and mean return per trade stays negative throughout. Not a tuning problem.

Removing all costs is the decisive diagnostic: mean gross return is still −0.083%/trade (profit factor 0.73). The signal has no edge before a penny of cost is charged. And average holding was 1.2 days — the "swing" method never actually swings, because the nearest safety line trails right under price and whips the position out.

05 — TRYING TO SAVE IT

The obvious fixes make it worse

The 1.2-day whipsaw points to the fragility of signalling off the last, steepest, newest line — on both entry and exit. Two fixes were tried, pre-registered.

A minimum line length (S = 20 days)

Forcing the action and safety lines to span at least a month gives trades room to breathe — holds rise to ~16 days, win rate to ~30%. But the edge gets monotonically worse as the lines grow longer, gross and net alike: a bigger move is needed to break a longer, shallower line, after which reversion is only stronger.

min span Sholdgross PFnet PF% profitable
5 d4.6 d0.800.630%
10 d8.7 d0.770.620%
20 d15.8 d0.720.570%
40 d26.8 d0.680.530%
60 d35.0 d0.650.490%
 Longer, more "established" lines → worse expectancy. No plateau, no lucky corner.

The author's exact exit (safety line only, no floor)

Tracking the bare safety line with no ATR floor is closer to what the author does. It reintroduces the whipsaw at short spans, and the 20-day minimum tames it — but at S = 20 it is numerically identical to the floored version (gross 0.72 / net 0.57). The exit rule doesn't matter, because the entries have no edge to protect.

06 — MULTI-TIMEFRAME

A coarser view of the same points

Wouldn't higher timeframes change the answer? Largely no: a weekly high is the maximum of that week's daily highs — coarser timeframes add no new price information, only a sparser set of the same extremes. And a higher-timeframe line is just a longer-span line — precisely the axis the S-sweep already walked, and it got monotonically worse. Multi-timeframe confluence can only select a subset of these signals, and every subset we could define lost. It is very unlikely to flip the sign.

07 — VERDICT

A clean negative result

On a single daily timeframe, this method has negative expectancy before costs, robust to the volatility band k, the length filter S, and the exit rule. The fragility fixes address the mechanism (whipsaw); none creates an edge.

Scope, honestly. This falsifies the faithful single-timeframe replication we could specify. It does not indict the author's full practice — live multi-timeframe reading and discretion sit outside what a mechanical test can capture. But nothing in the daily evidence points to those rescuing it, and the one structural lever they pull (longer/coarser lines) is the one we showed hurts.

It was a genuinely good idea to test — precise, mechanisable, plausible. The honest answer just turned out to be no.

08 — ADDENDUM

Does the entry geometry predict success?

A natural follow-up: is the probability of a trade winning a function of the setup — the gradients of the action and safety lines, their separation at entry, and their spans? To keep this from becoming a fishing expedition, every relationship was fit on the earlier half of ~11,900 trades and re-checked on the later half; the headline is a logistic model scored on the held-out half.

Win probability — yes, and it generalises

Three effects persist in both halves: a narrow action–safety separation (a tight channel), a shallow safety gradient, and low wedge convergence each raise the win rate. Together they score an out-of-sample AUC = 0.61 — about seven standard errors above chance, so this is real, generalising information. Ranked by the model's score, out-of-sample win rate climbs cleanly from the worst to the best geometry:

geometry decile (OOS)win rategross / tradenet / trade
1 — worst9.3%−0.089%−0.304%
514.8%−0.106%−0.322%
720.4%+0.007%−0.210%
925.1%+0.063%−0.154%
10 — best23.8%−0.007%−0.225%
 Out-of-sample. Win rate is genuinely sorted by the geometry; gross return is not.

Profit — no

The features sort whether a trade wins, not how much: their correlation with the trade return itself is ≈ 0. Tighter channels win more often but by smaller amounts, so even the best-geometry decile is only gross break-even (+0.06% at the very top), and after costs every decile is net-negative. You can predict the hit-rate; you cannot predict the payoff.

Volume behaves exactly the same

The README's other open question was volume: does a breakout on heavy volume mean more than one on light volume? Adding breakout-bar volume (relative to its 20-bar median) tells the identical story. It has ≈ 0 correlation with the trade return, so it does not predict move size — but it does modestly lift win probability (out-of-sample AUC rises 0.60 → 0.62; win rate climbs from 15% to 20% from the lowest to the highest volume quintile). Every volume quintile is still gross- and net-negative:

breakout-volume quintile (OOS)median vol×win %gross/tradenet/trade
1 — lowest0.68×15.4%−0.035%−0.251%
5 — highest2.03×19.7%−0.040%−0.256%
 Both things chart-traders trust to "confirm" a breakout — a clean setup and a volume surge — raise the odds of a win and change nothing about the payoff.

This is the study's most illuminating result. It shows why the method is such a consistent near-miss: the setups it selects are essentially random on expectancy. Every lever — channel geometry and volume — re-sorts whether a trade wins, never how much, so no filter built from them can turn the method profitable.

09 — FUTURES

A different instrument, a faded premium

Single equities are hostile ground for breakouts — they mean-revert. The author, though, reportedly trades futures, where trends genuinely persist. Re-run on a diversified 22-market basket — energy, metals, ags, rates, FX, plus the S&P and Nasdaq — over ~25 years, with futures costs (5 bps/side, no financing), the picture changes markedly.

The method is far more sympathetic here: base-case gross profit factor 0.97 versus 0.73 on equities, with 45% of markets gross-profitable on their own (silver +61%, cotton, soybeans, copper). And the minimum-span lever flips sign: on equities longer lines hurt, but on trending futures they help monotonically — letting trades ride trends instead of whipsawing. Across the full sample, net turns positive once the lines are long enough (S ≥ 40).

That out-of-sample split is the verdict. Trained on 2000–2012 and tested on 2013–2025:

min span Strain net PFtest net PFtest net/trade
401.090.99−0.020%
601.180.96−0.093%
 The strong in-sample edge does not survive into the later era; test-era gross is ~1.4 SE from zero — indistinguishable from nothing.

What the method-plus-long-span actually harvested was the time-series-momentum / managed- futures premium — a real, documented phenomenon that was strong through the 2000s commodity supercycle and has been largely absent since ~2012. Both of the natural instincts here — that the instrument matters and that a minimum timeframe matters — were correct and visible in the data. They just point at a premium that has faded, not a durable inefficiency.
